title: Recursion
subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
blurb: Trace a function calling itself: the stack, the base case, and why returns come back backwards.

concepts.name: How Function Calls Work
concepts.summary: A call pauses the caller, runs the callee, and hands back a single value to exactly the line where the call happened.
concepts.analogy: Leaving a bookmark in a book to go read a footnote - you come back to the exact line, not the top of the page.
key_ideas: a call transfers control and later returns it to the call site
a call evaluates to one return value
arguments are copied into the new call's own parameters
worked: main() runs, reaches the line `x = greet()`
greet() starts with its own fresh scope; main() is paused, not finished
greet() hits `return 'hi'`
control returns to main(), `x` becomes 'hi', execution continues on the next line

concepts.name: The Call Stack & Frames
concepts.summary: Every active call owns a frame holding its own parameters and locals. Frames are pushed on call and popped on return, last-in-first-out.
concepts.analogy: A stack of sticky notes: you can only add to the top and remove from the top.
key_ideas: each call gets its own separate frame
locals belong to a frame, they are not shared between calls
frames are removed in reverse order of creation
deep recursion grows the stack until it overflows
worked: call f(3) -> push frame [n=3]
f(3) calls f(2) -> push frame [n=2]; stack is now 3, 2
f(2) calls f(1) -> push frame [n=1]; stack is 3, 2, 1
f(1) returns -> pop n=1; f(2)'s frame is intact, still holding n=2

concepts.name: The Base Case
concepts.summary: The base case is a branch that returns without calling itself. Every chain of calls must be able to reach one.
concepts.analogy: The bottom rung of a ladder. Without it you keep climbing down with nothing to stop you.
key_ideas: the base case returns without recursing
it must be reachable from the initial call
every recursive path must eventually reach it
worked: write the recursive step: fact(n) = n * fact(n-1)
ask: what input can I answer without recursing? n <= 1 -> 1
check reachability: n-1 eventually reaches 1 for every n >= 1
test the edge: fact(0) must also return 1, so use `n <= 1`, not `n == 1`

concepts.name: The Recursive Case
concepts.summary: The recursive case solves a strictly smaller version of the same problem, and is allowed to assume that smaller call is already correct.
concepts.analogy: Standing in a queue and asking the person ahead of you for their position. You trust them to work out the rest.
key_ideas: each recursive call must receive a strictly smaller input
you may assume the recursive call returns the correct answer
the returned value must be combined and handed back
worked: goal: power(2, 3)
assume the smaller call works: power(2, 2) = 4
do the one step that turns it into the answer: 2 * 4 = 8
verify the input shrank: 3 -> 2, so this terminates

concepts.name: Return Values & Unwinding
concepts.summary: Returns happen in reverse order of the calls. The innermost call finishes first and its value flows outward one frame at a time.
concepts.analogy: Folding a stack of letters: the last one written is the first one read.
key_ideas: returns occur in reverse call order
each frame receives the value returned by the call it made
a returned value is lost if the caller does not use it
worked: f(3) calls f(2), which calls f(1), which returns 1
that 1 lands in f(2)'s frame; f(2) computes 2 + 1 and returns 3
that 3 lands in f(3)'s frame; f(3) computes 3 + 3 and returns 6
notice: the values come back in reverse order of the calls, one frame at a time

concepts.name: Recursion Trees
concepts.summary: A call that makes more than one recursive call produces a branching tree. Total work is the number of nodes, not the depth.
concepts.analogy: A family tree where everyone has two children. The bottom row is enormous even though the tree is short.
key_ideas: branching factor drives total call count
total work is the number of nodes
depth still governs stack memory
worked: fib(5) calls fib(4) and fib(3)
fib(4) calls fib(3) and fib(2) - note fib(3) is computed twice already
level 0 has 1 node, level 1 has 2, level 2 has 4, level 3 has 8
total nodes for depth d is about 2^d, which is why fib(40) hangs

concepts.name: Time & Space Complexity
concepts.summary: Recursion always spends stack space proportional to its maximum depth, even when its time cost is good.
concepts.analogy: A chain of phone calls: even if only one person is talking, everybody stays on the line.
key_ideas: space is proportional to maximum depth
time is driven by how many calls are made
memoization trades space to buy back time
worked: sum_to(n) recurses to depth n before returning anything
at the deepest point the stack holds n frames - that is O(n) space
the number of calls is also n - that is O(n) time
rewrite as a loop and the frames disappear: O(n) time, O(1) space

concepts.name: Memoization
concepts.summary: Cache the results of subproblems you have already solved. It only pays off when the same subproblem is reached repeatedly.
concepts.analogy: Writing answers on a sticky note so you never redo the same sum twice.
key_ideas: it requires overlapping subproblems
the cache is keyed by the arguments
it collapses an exponential tree into a linear chain of unique states
worked: fib(5) -> fib(4), fib(3)
fib(4) -> fib(3), fib(2)   <-- fib(3) is now being recomputed
store fib(3) in a dict the first time you compute it
the second request for fib(3) is a dict lookup, not a subtree
the exponential tree collapses into a linear chain of n+1 unique values

concepts.name: Tail Recursion & Stack Depth
concepts.summary: A call is tail-recursive when the recursive call is the final action and its result is returned unchanged. Some languages reclaim the frame; Python does not.
concepts.analogy: Handing over a baton at the end of a lap. There is nothing left to remember about the previous lap.
key_ideas: the recursive call must be the last operation
its value must be returned directly, not combined afterwards
tail-call optimisation is a language feature, never automatic in Python
worked: non-tail: return n * f(n-1) - the multiplication happens after the call returns
tail:     return f(n-1, acc+n) - nothing happens after the call returns
in tail position the current frame has no remaining work
so a runtime that supports TCO can reuse the frame instead of pushing a new one
CPython does not do this, so Python still raises RecursionError at the limit

misconceptions.name: Recursion stops on its own
misconceptions.statement: A recursive function terminates as long as it looks like it is getting smaller, so an explicit base case is optional.
misconceptions.why: Termination requires that some call actually returns without recursing. If none does, the chain continues until the stack overflows - the base case is not a formality, it is the only thing that ends the process.
misconceptions.repair: Find the branch that returns a plain value. If there is none, you have written an infinite chain, not a recursion.

misconceptions.name: Recursive calls share one set of variables
misconceptions.statement: All the calls are working on the same variable, so changing it in one call changes it everywhere.
misconceptions.why: Each call gets its own frame. The parameter in one call is a different variable from the parameter in another, even though they share a name.
misconceptions.repair: Picture the stack: n=3, then n=2, then n=1, each in its own box. When n=2 returns, the n=3 box still holds 3.

misconceptions.name: Returns come back in the order they were called
misconceptions.statement: If f(3) called f(2) first, then f(3) returns first too.
misconceptions.why: Calls go down the stack and returns come back up it, so the order reverses. The innermost call is the first to finish and the last to be made.
misconceptions.repair: Read the print statements in two passes: everything before the recursive call prints on the way down, everything after prints on the way up, reversed.

misconceptions.name: The recursive result comes back automatically
misconceptions.statement: You can just call the function recursively and the answer will find its way to the caller.
misconceptions.why: A return value only reaches the caller if the caller uses it - by returning it, storing it, or combining it. A bare call throws the value away.
misconceptions.repair: Every recursive call must appear inside a return, or be assigned to something that is later returned.

misconceptions.name: Recursion costs no extra memory
misconceptions.statement: Recursion is just a compact way of writing a loop, so it uses no additional memory.
misconceptions.why: Every call that has not returned yet is holding a live frame. Memory grows with maximum depth, which is why deep recursion can overflow.
misconceptions.repair: Count the boxes on the stack at the deepest point. That count is your space complexity.

misconceptions.name: Two recursive calls still mean linear time
misconceptions.statement: A function with two recursive calls just does twice the work per level, so it is still O(n).
misconceptions.why: Two calls per level means the number of calls doubles at every level: 1, 2, 4, 8 ... That is 2^depth total calls, which is exponential, not linear.
misconceptions.repair: Draw the call tree for n=4 and count the nodes. If each level doubles, the total is exponential.

misconceptions.name: Memoization speeds up any recursion
misconceptions.statement: Adding a cache makes any recursive function faster.
misconceptions.why: A cache only helps if the same subproblem is reached more than once. If every subproblem is unique the cache never hits, and you have added overhead for nothing.
misconceptions.repair: Ask whether two different paths can arrive at the same arguments. If not, there is nothing to cache.

misconceptions.name: Tail recursion is optimised automatically
misconceptions.statement: Writing the recursive call last means the interpreter will optimise it into a loop.
misconceptions.why: Tail-call optimisation is a property of the language and compiler. Python has no TCO and enforces a recursion limit, so a tail-recursive Python function still overflows.
misconceptions.repair: Tail position is necessary but not sufficient - check whether your runtime actually performs TCO.

items.stem: What happens the moment `greet()` is called from inside `main()`?

options.text: Control jumps to greet(); when it returns, main() resumes at the exact next line
main() keeps running at the same time as greet()
greet() runs, then the whole program restarts from the top
greet() runs but main() never receives a value back

items.explain: A call is a detour, not a fork. Control moves to the callee, and on return it lands on the line immediately after the call.

items.stem: Given `def add(a, b): return a + b`, what does the expression `add(x, y)` evaluate to?

options.text: A single value - whatever the return statement produced
Nothing; you have to print inside the function to get a value
The function object itself
Both a and b, returned together

items.explain: A call expression is replaced by its return value at the call site. That is what makes `z = add(2,3)` meaningful.

items.stem: A function `f(n)` calls `f(n-1)` but contains no return statement. What does `f(5)` evaluate to?

options.text: None - the recursion runs but no value ever comes back
The result of f(4)
An error, because recursion requires a return

items.explain: The call happens, the work happens, and then the value is dropped on the floor. No return means the call evaluates to None.

items.stem: `f(3)` calls `f(2)` which calls `f(1)`. How many frames are on the stack at the moment `f(1)` starts executing?

options.text: 3 - one for each call that has not returned yet
1 - only the currently executing call matters
0 - recursion does not use the stack
6 - one for each call and each return

items.explain: Frames accumulate on the way down. At the deepest point all three calls are still live, so all three frames exist.

items.stem: Each call of `f(n)` has a local `total`. `f(3)` sets total=3, then calls `f(2)`, which sets total=2. When `f(2)` returns, what is `total` in the `f(3)` frame?

options.text: 3 - each frame has its own total
2 - the most recent assignment wins
0 - locals are reset when a call returns
It depends on whether total was passed as an argument

items.explain: This is the single most common recursion bug. The inner frame's total is a different variable, and it disappears when that frame is popped.

items.stem: Why does `f(n) = f(n-1) + 1` with no base case crash with RecursionError instead of looping forever?

options.text: Each call pushes a frame, and the stack has a finite size, so it overflows
Python detects the missing base case and stops it
n eventually becomes negative and Python rejects negative input
Recursion uses no memory, so it hits a CPU limit instead

items.explain: The crash is a stack overflow, not a cleverness on the interpreter's part. That distinction matters because it tells you the fix is structural.

items.stem: In `def fact(n):` / `if n <= 1: return 1` / `return n * fact(n-1)` - which line makes termination possible?

options.text: `if n <= 1: return 1` - it returns without calling itself
`return n * fact(n-1)` - it calls itself with a smaller n
Both lines share the responsibility equally
Neither; this needs a loop to terminate

items.explain: Shrinking the input is necessary but not sufficient. Something has to stop the shrinking by returning.

items.stem: Consider `def count(n): if n == 0: return 0; return count(n-2)`. What happens when you call `count(5)`?

options.text: It never reaches 0, so it recurses until the stack overflows
It returns 0, because 5 is close enough to 0
It stops at n=1 because Python rounds down
It raises a TypeError on odd numbers

items.explain: 5, 3, 1, -1, -3 ... the base case is never hit. A base case only helps if the recursive step can actually reach it.

items.stem: A recursive function has a correct base case, but for some inputs the recursive call does not shrink the input. What is the symptom?

options.text: Infinite recursion for those inputs only - the base case is unreachable from them
It cannot happen; a base case guarantees termination
The base case is skipped but the loop still ends
Python raises a ValueError before it runs

items.explain: Correctness of the base case is a per-input property. You must show that every input path leads to it, which is the real content of a termination proof.

items.stem: In `def power(x, n): if n == 0: return 1; return x * power(x, n-1)`, what is the job of `x * power(x, n-1)`?

options.text: It trusts the smaller call to produce x^(n-1), then builds x^n from it
It loops n times multiplying x
It launches n calls in parallel
It returns the smaller answer unchanged

items.explain: This is the leap of faith: assume the smaller call is correct, then do the one step that turns it into your answer.

items.stem: `def total(lst): return lst[0] + total(lst)` - why is the recursive case invalid?

options.text: It passes the same list, so the input never gets smaller
It adds lst[0] twice
It is missing a base case
Lists cannot be passed to recursive functions

items.explain: The subproblem must be strictly smaller. `lst[1:]` would be a valid recursive step; `lst` is not.

items.stem: `def sum_to(n): if n == 0: return 0; return sum_to(n-1)` - the base case is fine. What is wrong?

options.text: n is never added, so it always returns 0
Nothing is wrong; it returns the sum
It recurses infinitely
The base case returns the wrong type

items.explain: The value comes back up the stack correctly, but every frame passes it along untouched. The combining step is missing.

items.stem: `f(3)` calls `f(2)` calls `f(1)`, and each one prints `n` *after* its recursive call. What order prints?

options.text: 1 2 3 - the innermost call finishes first
3 2 1 - the same order the calls were made
3 2 1 then 1 2 3
Only 1 - the outer prints are skipped

items.explain: Code before the call runs on the way down; code after the call runs on the way up, which is reversed.

items.stem: In `def f(n): if n == 0: return 0; f(n-1); return n` - what does `f(3)` return?

options.text: 3 - the inner result is discarded, then n is returned
0 - the base case value bubbles all the way up
6 - the values are summed while unwinding
Nothing, because the inner call returns first

items.explain: `f(n-1)` is called and its value is thrown away. Each frame returns its own n, so the outermost value wins.

items.stem: Why does `return n + f(n-1)` give the right answer while `f(n-1); return n` does not?

options.text: Only the first hands the inner result back outward; the second discards it
The first is faster and finishes before unwinding
The second is missing a base case
The second returns n before the inner call runs

items.explain: Unwinding is a relay, not a broadcast. Each frame must explicitly pass the baton to the frame that called it.

items.stem: `fib(n)` calls both `fib(n-1)` and `fib(n-2)`. Roughly how many calls happen for `fib(5)`?

options.text: About 15 - the calls form a branching tree
About 5 - one per level of recursion
About 10 - two per level
Exactly 2

items.explain: The tree branches, so the count is closer to phi^5 than to 5. Draw it and count the nodes.

items.stem: A function makes 2 recursive calls per invocation and bottoms out at depth 10. Total calls are on the order of:

options.text: 2^10 - the tree doubles at every level
20 - two calls times ten levels
10 - depth is what matters
100 - ten squared

items.explain: 1, 2, 4, 8 ... doubling per level is exponentiation. This is exactly why naive fib is unusable for large n.

items.stem: Recursion depth is only 20, but the function makes 2 calls per level and takes 3 seconds. Why?

options.text: The tree has roughly a million nodes - depth is small but total work is exponential
Deep recursion is always slow because the stack is large
Python's recursion limit is being hit
Two calls per level means 40 calls total

items.explain: Depth and total work are different quantities. This is the distinction that separates a fast recursion from a slow one.

items.stem: What is the space complexity of a recursion that goes n levels deep and allocates nothing extra?

options.text: O(n) - one frame per live call
O(1) - recursion adds no memory
O(n^2) - frames are copied at each level
O(log n) - the stack halves each time

items.explain: Stack space is the cost recursion almost always charges, even when it is a model of elegance otherwise.

items.stem: Naive `fib(n)` is O(2^n) in time. What is its space complexity?

options.text: O(n) - only one root-to-leaf path is on the stack at a time
O(2^n) - the same as time, since every call allocates

items.explain: Frames are popped as the tree is explored depth-first, so peak memory tracks depth, not node count. A common interview question for exactly this reason.

items.stem: A recursive `sum(lst)` is O(n) time and O(n) space, while a loop version is O(n) time and O(1) space. Why?

options.text: The recursive version keeps n frames alive; the loop keeps none
The recursive version copies the list at every call
They have identical space; recursion never costs extra memory
The loop is faster because it uses the CPU cache

items.explain: This is the honest trade-off. Recursion buys clarity with stack memory, and knowing that is what lets you choose deliberately.

items.stem: Memoized `fib(n)` drops from O(2^n) to O(n). What makes that possible?

options.text: The same subproblems recur many times, and the cache returns them instantly
The cache stores the whole call tree so it never recurses
Memoization removes the need for a base case
It runs the two branches in parallel

items.explain: There are only n+1 distinct fib values but exponentially many paths to them. The cache collapses the paths into the values.

items.stem: You memoize a recursive function that sums a list by splitting it in half. Does it help?

options.text: Barely - every subproblem is unique, so the cache never hits
Yes, it halves the runtime
Yes, it becomes O(1)
No, memoization never works on lists

items.explain: Overlapping subproblems are the precondition, not a bonus. Without repeats you have added a dict lookup to every call for nothing.

items.stem: For memoization to be correct and not just fast, what must hold?

options.text: The same arguments must always produce the same result - no dependence on outside mutable state
The arguments must be small integers
The function must be tail-recursive
The base case must be at 0

items.explain: Caching assumes referential transparency. If the function reads a global that changes, the cache will hand back stale answers.

items.stem: Which of these is tail-recursive?

options.text: `def f(n, acc): return acc if n == 0 else f(n-1, acc+n)`
`def f(n): return 1 if n == 0 else n * f(n-1)`
`def f(n): return 0 if n == 0 else n + f(n-1)`
The last two are both tail-recursive

items.explain: In the first, the recursive call's value is returned untouched. In the others, a multiplication or addition happens after the call returns, so the frame must survive.

items.stem: Does Python optimise tail recursion?

options.text: No - Python has a recursion limit and performs no tail-call optimisation
Yes, since Python 3.8
Yes, if you decorate the function with @tailcall
Only for integer arguments

items.explain: This trips people up constantly. Writing a function in tail position does nothing for you in CPython; the stack still grows.

items.stem: Why can a tail-recursive function theoretically run in constant stack space?

options.text: Nothing remains to be done after the call returns, so the caller's frame can be replaced
Because tail recursion always has a smaller input
Because the compiler rewrites it as a loop only when there is one argument
Because tail calls skip the base case

items.explain: The frame exists to remember what to do next. In tail position there is nothing to remember, so the frame is disposable.
